reports.title: Highlights of Consumer Price Index (CPI) Rebasing
reports.description: VERIFIED DIRECTLY this session via NBS's own 'Highlights of CPI Rebasing' document (February 2025, downloaded and text-extracted directly since WebFetch could not render the PDF's binary content on the first attempt). States plainly: 'The Jevon elementary Index is preferred to Dutot, because it passes all four economic criteria which are Transitivity, Reversibility, Commensurability and Proportionality' -- confirming the docx's and Grok's claimed formula switch with NBS's own stated reasoning, which neither the docx nor Grok's round had actually quoted. Classification: 'According to the Classification of Individual Consumption According to Purpose (COICOP) version 2018, there are 13 Divisions used for CPI computation, ... 45 Groups, 100 Classes, 164 Subclasses, and 242 item-level observations' tracking 934 product varieties. 'The weight reference period is now 2023, and the price reference period (Base year) is 2024.' Weights sourced from 'the 2023 Nigeria Living Standards Survey (NLSS) and the 2024 Survey of Rare Items', supplemented by administrative data from the Central Bank of Nigeria, NAICOM, and NBS's own National Accounts and Trade Statistics divisions; 'the household expenditure data used for the weighting were purely monetary.' Higher-level aggregation: 'the index is computed using the Modified Laspeyres method (Young Index).' Replaces a 2009-base series. The 12-month index-reference-period-maximisation detail (from the docx, attributed to IMF CPI Manual Sec. 9.125 and the still-unconfirmed ECOWAS HCPI framework) does not appear in this particular document and was not independently located elsewhere this session -- likely a later refinement (per the docx, 'around the December 2025 figures'), not part of the original February 2025 rebasing announcement.
reports.cadence_note: Recurs only when the NBS re-bases the CPI — a one-off special report per rebasing, not the monthly CPI series it sat mis-cadenced against until 2026-08-12 (it had inherited releases_per_year: 12 from that separate series). Historical rebasing gaps run 9–20 years (2009, then February 2025), so 0.1/year is a nominal rate per the sna-2008 convention (Thomas's Q2 ruling): a deliberate stand-in that keeps the pulse slow and honest. The monthly CPI series itself is not yet a node — first item for the Africa branch, per Thomas's 2026-08-12 direction to treat the two as separate nodes.

release_schedule.note: This report documents the results of a CPI 'rebasing' exercise (updating the price/weight reference base year), which NBS Nigeria conducts at irregular multi-year intervals, not on a fixed calendar. The most recent rebasing was released in February 2025 (weight reference 2023, price reference/base year 2024), replacing the prior 2009 base year — a 15-year gap. Historically, NBS's GDP/CPI rebasing exercises have occurred at inconsistent intervals (20 years, then 9 years, per NBS official Dr. Baba Madu). The UN Statistical Commission recommends rebasing every 5-10 years, but Nigeria has not followed a consistent cadence, and no next rebasing date has been announced. This is a special/periodic report, not the regular monthly CPI release (which is a separate NBS publication).

reports.title: Pension Reform Act, 2014
reports.description: Nigeria's framework pension statute. Section 15(4) is quoted directly in PenCom's own December 2025 circular (VERIFIED DIRECTLY this session): 'Section 15(4) of the Pension Reform Act (PRA) 2014 guarantees the right of retirees of the Public Service of the Federation to pension review.' Section 53 is separately invoked, per Grok's round (secondary, via PenCom statements as reported in press coverage, not independently quoted from the Act itself or a primary circular) as the basis for PenCom's enforcement action increasing legacy NSITF pensions -- see ng-nsitf-legacy-pension-enforcement. Neither section prescribes a CPI or inflation-based formula; both require periodic review without specifying the method, leaving quantum and timing to administrative determination -- the same shape as the Constitution's own s.173(3) (quoted in full under ng-pencom-federal-pension-review-circular), which requires review 'every five years or together with any Federal Civil Service salary reviews, whichever is earlier' but not a calculation method.

reports.title: Circular on Pension Increases for Federal Government Self-Funded Agencies
reports.description: VERIFIED DIRECTLY this session (direct fetch of the circular itself, issued 8 December 2025). States its legal basis in full: 'Section 173(3) of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 (as amended) provides that pension of the Federal Public Servants shall be reviewed every five years or together with any Federal Civil Service salary reviews, whichever is earlier. In addition, Section 15(4) of the Pension Reform Act (PRA) 2014 guarantees the right of retirees of the Public Service of the Federation to pension review.' Critically, the circular does NOT contain a CPI or inflation-based formula: it instead references six prior circulars from the National Salaries, Incomes and Wages Commission carrying specific negotiated rates (15%, 33%, 20%, 28%) and a fixed monthly adjustment (N32,000), none tied to a stated CPI calculation. A clean confirmation of Nigeria's general shape across this whole slice: statutory review obligations are real and periodically enforced, but the review quantum is negotiated/administrative rather than automatically calculated from any published price index.
reports.cadence_note: Triggered by the five-year/salary-review cycle in Constitution s.173(3), not a fixed annual cadence.

release_schedule.rule: Section 173(3) of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 (as amended) provides that pension of Federal Public Servants shall be reviewed every five years or together with any Federal Civil Service salary review, whichever is earlier.
release_schedule.note: The 8 December 2025 PenCom circular (implementing pension increases for Self-Funded Agencies) confirms this rule verbatim but does not state a next review date. Because the trigger is 'every five years OR any ad-hoc salary review, whichever is earlier', and salary reviews occur unpredictably, no fixed next date is computable — consistent with the existing cadence_note on file.

reports.title: NSITF Legacy Pension Enhancement (PenCom enforcement action)
reports.description: Grok-sourced (secondary, via PenCom statements as reported in contemporaneous press coverage; no downloadable primary circular located by either half of the split -- see _open_questions). Around late January 2026, PenCom directed an increase in legacy pensions for retirees of the former Nigeria Social Insurance Trust Fund (NSITF) scheme, reportedly the first increase since 2005: aggregate monthly payments across 2,116 verified retirees rising from roughly N12.56 million to N159.95 million, with N8.70 billion in arrears paid. Legal basis invoked: Section 53 of the Pension Reform Act 2014 (see ng-pension-reform-act-2014), following PenCom's own account of enforcing compliance after a prolonged administrative freeze. Reported as made possible by NSITF Fund growth (from N54 billion at the 2005 transfer to N195 billion by December 2025) rather than by any CPI calculation -- described in every source found as a discretionary catch-up quantum, not an automatic indexation formula.

reports.title: National Social Safety Net Program - Scale Up (NASSP-SU), incl. Economic Shock Responsive Cash Transfer (ESR-CT)
reports.description: VERIFIED DIRECTLY this session, quoting the project's own text (P176935): development objective 'Expand coverage of shock responsive safety net support among the poor and vulnerable and strengthen the national safety net delivery system.' US$800 million total project cost, with the World Bank's IDA financing covering the full US$800 million per this session's own fetch of a procurement-strategy document (no Nigerian government counterpart financing identified in that document; Grok's round separately gives a household transfer figure of roughly N25,000/month over 6 months for the Economic Shock Responsive Cash Transfer component, not independently confirmed by this session's own fetch, which instead surfaced unit-cost line items for a 6-month, N53/beneficiary procurement category whose relationship to the actual household benefit level is unclear). Approved 16 December 2021, effective January 2023. Responds to 'rising food prices and inflation' in its own framing but is explicitly time-limited and shock-triggered rather than an ongoing CPI-indexed benefit -- see _dropped for why no edge connects this to ng-nbs-cpi-rebasing.

dependencies.basis: The circular quotes its own statutory basis directly: 'Section 15(4) of the Pension Reform Act (PRA) 2014 guarantees the right of retirees of the Public Service of the Federation to pension review.'

NBS's own Highlights document: 'According to the Classification of Individual Consumption According to Purpose (COICOP) version 2018, there are 13 Divisions used for CPI computation.' Reuses the un-coicop-2018 node already carried by South Africa, Kenya and Ghana -- Nigeria is in fact the country whose own docx entry first named COICOP 2018 explicitly among this branch's raw material, now independently confirmed at the primary-document level.

VERIFIED DIRECTLY this session: the IMF's own press release (No. 16/75, dated 24 February 2016) is titled 'Nigeria to Implement the IMF's Enhanced General Data Dissemination System' -- confirming Nigeria's e-GDDS implementation date (full press-release body text was not extractable, so this rests on the confirmed title, number and date rather than a quoted passage; Grok's round separately gives a National Summary Data Page live date of March 2016, consistent with an implementation announced the preceding month). Nigeria is now a fourth country in this branch confirmed on the weaker e-GDDS tier, after Kenya, Ethiopia and Ghana.

_dropped.why: NASSP-SU/ESR-CT is framed as a response to 'rising food prices and inflation' but per Grok's round has no stated formula tying the transfer amount to CPI -- it is a time-limited, shock-triggered programme rather than an ongoing CPI-indexed benefit, structurally different from Ghana's LEAP (a real formula) and Ethiopia's PSNP5/UPSNJP (real formulas, one suspended). This is the first case in the branch of a safety-net programme explicitly motivated by inflation but NOT mechanically linked to the CPI series that measures it.

Per Grok's round: the National Minimum Wage Act, 2019 sets up a Tripartite Committee review process (historically ~5-year cycles, moving toward ~3-year per recent practice) with no automatic CPI-indexation formula written into the Act. Organised labour has publicly called for annual inflation-linked adjustment referencing NBS CPI, but this has not been enacted. No node minted at all (not just not-edged) -- same treatment as Ghana's minimum wage in gh-leap-cpi-indexation.json, for the same reason: a negotiated outcome, not a documented computational dependency.
